title: Morning Edition
dek: An AI-led market selloff, Japan's fiscal choices, ancient chemistry, and the deep sea's hidden food webs.

lead_story.headline: Global stocks slide as AI investment fears spread across Asia
lead_story.summary: Asian markets followed Wall Street's sharp November 5 selloff, with Japan and South Korea losing around 6% on Friday. Investors are reassessing expensive AI-linked stocks and the borrowing behind data-centre expansion; market moves do not prove that AI demand has collapsed.
lead_story.why_it_matters: The selloff tests assumptions about how much growth and cash flow can justify enormous AI infrastructure commitments.

items.headline: Japan proposes using central-bank asset-sale proceeds for strategic investment
items.summary: Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi outlined plans to redirect additional proceeds from the Bank of Japan's exchange-traded fund sales toward growth and economic-security priorities. The BOJ says sales will remain gradual and independent.
items.why_it_matters: The plan links unusual central-bank holdings to fiscal choices at a time of market stress; it is a proposal, not completed spending.

items.headline: Oil market shows early signs of surplus despite Middle East disruption
items.summary: Reuters reports recovering Gulf exports and weaker demand are easing a previously tight physical oil market. Bank estimates differ and refined-product flows remain disrupted by the Iran war.
items.why_it_matters: Price signals and refinery bottlenecks can diverge, complicating inflation forecasts and energy-security decisions.

items.headline: Siberian tomb offers disputed clues to ancient cannabis use
items.summary: Researchers studying a 2,800-year-old Scythian-era burial found cannabis seeds and chemical evidence in preserved hair. The team argues this may show psychoactive use, but a forensic specialist questions whether the hair proves consumption rather than environmental exposure.
items.why_it_matters: The study illustrates how archaeological chemistry can extend knowledge of past behavior—and how contamination and interpretation limit certainty.

items.headline: European flight disruptions follow a wave of false bomb threats
items.summary: At least 25 commercial flights across Europe were disrupted Thursday by threats that proved false. Investigators are examining possible coordination; purported attribution in some emails has not been substantiated.
items.why_it_matters: The incident illustrates the operational cost of threats even when no explosives are found, without evidence to assign responsibility.

items.headline: Older catch-up: a levitated magnet tests an extreme dark-matter hypothesis
items.summary: Rice University researchers used a suspended magnet to search for interactions with unusually massive dark-matter candidates. They detected no signal but narrowed some possible interaction strengths; the work was presented at a conference.
items.why_it_matters: Negative results are part of scientific progress when an experiment rules out previously plausible regions of a search.

items.headline: A Texas library holds a Thanksgiving-themed reading night—with a turkey pardon
items.summary: Plainview's Caprock Community Literacy Council scheduled its First Thursday Reading Night for November 5 at Unger Memorial Library, with children's crafts, a book giveaway and a mayoral turkey pardon. This is an event announcement, not independent confirmation of attendance.
items.why_it_matters: The event offers a glimpse of local civic rituals that exist alongside national political and economic upheaval.

items.headline: Zhuangzi's challenge to the belief that success is deserved
items.summary: Philosopher Christine Abigail L Tan examines Zhuangzi's criticism of meritocracy: achievement depends on contingent circumstances and relationships, not simply isolated individual virtue or effort.
items.why_it_matters: The essay offers a non-Western framework for discussing opportunity, humility and how societies distribute esteem.

worth_your_time.headline: A whale-fall graveyard reveals a deep-sea ecosystem on an immense scale
worth_your_time.summary: A Nature News & Views analysis describes research identifying a roughly 1,200-kilometre-long region of accumulated whale remains along the Diamantina fracture zone in the Indian Ocean. The interpretation raises questions about deep-sea nutrient supply and preservation.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: It offers a rare view of how large animal deaths can sustain ecosystems far below sunlight, and how researchers reconstruct inaccessible habitats.

daily_wonder.title: A snow crystal, photographed before the digital age
daily_wonder.caption: Wilson A. Bentley made thousands of photographs of individual snow crystals in Vermont, revealing their intricate branching symmetry. This historical photomicrograph records one crystal, not a computer-generated pattern.
daily_wonder.alt: Black-and-white microscopic photograph of a single branching sixfold snow crystal against a dark background.

reflection.passage: We are such stuff / As dreams are made on
reflection.author: William Shakespeare
reflection.context: Prospero speaks after the magical masque disappears. He reflects on the fragility of pageantry, worldly grandeur and human life; the passage is not simply a celebration of imagination.
reflection.question: What in ordinary life feels permanent only because we rarely imagine its ending?
